marks: Cao Quỳnh Cư, Cao Hoài Sang, Lê Văn Trung and Phạm Công Tắc founded the Spiritualist club AĂÂ here to practise mediumship.
The religion was officially established in this city in 1926; the Holy See and its Great Divine Temple stand here.
Caodaist leaders were jailed in French penal colonies here from 1941 to 1946.
notes: A group of colonial clerks in Saigon found the Spiritualist club AĂÂ to practise mediumship and ouija sessions.
After a séance revelation, Ngô Văn Chiêu signs the Declaration of the Founding of the Cao Đài Religion on 7 October, and the religion is officially established at Tây Ninh.

Lê Văn Trung, the first and only ordained Pope of the Tây Ninh Holy See, dies; Phạm Công Tắc assumes the role. From 1934 to 1975 the religion splits into independent sects, sometimes as many as thirty.
The religion has over a million members, a fifth to a quarter of the population of Cochinchina.
Phạm Công Tắc and other leaders are arrested and jailed in French penal colonies in Madagascar until 1946.
Members of Cao Đài, active in the Indochina Wars, are repressed after the fall of Saigon, and the communist government bans the practice of Caodaism.
Caodaism is granted legal recognition and unrestricted practice once again; the Tây Ninh Executive Council is officially recognised.
About 2.5 million Caodaists are estimated in Vietnam by the United Nations (January 2015), with tens of thousands in a diaspora in North America, Cambodia, Europe and Australia.
src: Blagov, Sergei A. (2012). Caodaism: Vietnamese Traditionalism and Its Leap Into Modernity. Nova Science Publishers.
